source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Discrete random variable and sample space
statement: A chance experiment may be modeled by a random variable whose possible outcomes form the sample space; the random variable is discrete when this space is finite or countably infinite.
conditions: An experiment has outcomes depending on chance.
The set of possible outcomes is finite or countably infinite.
conclusion: The outcome variable is a discrete random variable with that set as its sample space.
typical_uses: Check that sums over outcomes are legitimate in a discrete probability argument.
Repair proofs that use event probabilities before specifying the relevant sample space.
common_misuses: Treating an uncountable outcome space as discrete without a density or measure.
Confusing the random variable with a particular realized outcome.
bridge_lemmas: Events are subsets of the sample space.
Singleton outcomes are elements of the sample space.
repair_templates: State the sample space and verify it is finite or countably infinite before applying discrete formulas.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Discrete distribution function
statement: On a finite sample space, a distribution function assigns nonnegative masses summing to 1, and the probability of an event is the sum of the masses of its outcomes.
conditions: Omega is a finite sample space.
m(omega) >= 0 for every omega in Omega.
The sum of m(omega) over Omega is 1.
E is a subset of Omega.
conclusion: P(E) equals the sum of m(omega) over omega in E.
typical_uses: Compute event probabilities by summing elementary outcome probabilities.
Check whether a proposed finite probability model is normalized.
common_misuses: Forgetting to prove that all masses are nonnegative.
Using equal masses without justifying uniformity.
Summing over outcomes outside the event.
bridge_lemmas: P({omega}) = m(omega) for each outcome omega.
A finite sum over the empty event is 0.
repair_templates: Add a normalization check and rewrite the event as a set of outcomes before summing masses.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Basic finite probability properties
statement: Probabilities from a finite distribution are nonnegative, assign probability 1 to the sample space, are monotone under inclusion, add over disjoint unions, and satisfy the complement formula.
conditions: P is defined from a finite distribution function on Omega.
A, B, E, and F are events in Omega.
For additivity, A and B are disjoint.
For monotonicity, E is a subset of F.
conclusion: P(E) >= 0, P(Omega) = 1, P(E) <= P(F), P(A union B) = P(A)+P(B), and P(A complement) = 1-P(A), as applicable.
typical_uses: Repair elementary probability calculations that omit complements, monotonicity, or disjointness checks.
Detect invalid addition of probabilities for overlapping events.
common_misuses: Adding P(A)+P(B) when A and B overlap.
Using P(A complement)=1-P(A) relative to the wrong sample space.
Inferring equality of probabilities from set inclusion alone.
bridge_lemmas: A and its complement are disjoint and have union Omega.
If E is a subset of F, then F is the disjoint union of E and F minus E.
repair_templates: If events overlap, replace the disjoint-addition step with inclusion-exclusion or split the events into disjoint parts.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite additivity over pairwise disjoint events
statement: The probability of a finite union of pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their probabilities.
conditions: A1,...,An are events in the same sample space.
The events A1,...,An are pairwise disjoint.
P is a probability on that sample space.
conclusion: P(A1 union ... union An) = sum_i P(Ai).
typical_uses: Check total probability decompositions and case splits.
Repair proofs by replacing overlapping cases with pairwise disjoint cases.
common_misuses: Using finite additivity when the listed events overlap.
Omitting a case from the union.
Assuming pairwise disjointness from distinct labels.
bridge_lemmas: Pairwise disjoint means Ai intersect Aj is empty for i != j.
Each outcome in the union belongs to exactly one Ai.
repair_templates: Verify disjointness or refine the cases to Ai minus earlier cases before summing probabilities.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Partition decomposition of an event
statement: If a finite family of disjoint events partitions the sample space, then the probability of any event is the sum of the probabilities of its intersections with the partition cells.
conditions: A1,...,An are pairwise disjoint events.
Omega = A1 union ... union An.
E is an event in Omega.
conclusion: P(E) = sum_i P(E intersect Ai).
typical_uses: Justify splitting a probability calculation into exhaustive cases.
Repair missing case analysis in conditional probability and Bayes arguments.
common_misuses: Using a family that is not exhaustive.
Dropping intersections with E when summing over cases.
Counting a case twice because the cases are not disjoint.
bridge_lemmas: The events E intersect Ai are pairwise disjoint.
The union of E intersect Ai over all i equals E.
repair_templates: State the partition explicitly, then replace E by the disjoint union of E intersect Ai.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Split an event by another event
statement: Any event A can be split into the disjoint parts where B occurs and where B does not occur.
conditions: A and B are events in the same sample space.
conclusion: P(A) = P(A intersect B) + P(A intersect B complement).
typical_uses: Repair arguments that condition on whether B happened.
Check calculations using a binary case split.
common_misuses: Forgetting the complement case.
Assuming A intersect B and A intersect B complement have equal probability.
Using the formula with complements taken in different sample spaces.
bridge_lemmas: B and B complement partition Omega.
A intersect B and A intersect B complement are disjoint and union to A.
repair_templates: Insert the missing complementary case and verify both pieces are evaluated in the same probability space.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Two-event inclusion-exclusion
statement: For two events, the probability of their union equals the sum of their probabilities minus the probability of their intersection.
conditions: A and B are events in the same sample space.
conclusion: P(A union B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersect B).
typical_uses: Repair invalid addition of probabilities for overlapping events.
Check union computations in finite probability models.
common_misuses: Subtracting P(A intersect B) when A and B are already disjoint is harmless but often signals unnecessary work.
Forgetting to subtract the overlap.
Replacing intersection by union in the correction term.
bridge_lemmas: An outcome in both A and B is counted twice by P(A)+P(B).
If A and B are disjoint, the intersection term is 0.
repair_templates: When a proof adds P(A) and P(B), add a disjointness proof or subtract P(A intersect B).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Uniform distribution on a finite sample space
statement: On a sample space with n outcomes, the uniform distribution assigns mass 1/n to every outcome.
conditions: Omega is a finite sample space with n elements.
Each outcome is intended to be equally likely.
conclusion: For every omega in Omega, m(omega)=1/n, and P(E)=|E|/n for each event E.
typical_uses: Convert counting arguments into probabilities.
Check fair dice, fair cards, and equally likely finite models.
common_misuses: Using |E|/n when outcomes are not equally likely.
Choosing a sample space whose elements are not equally likely and then applying the uniform formula.
bridge_lemmas: If all n masses are equal and sum to 1, each mass is 1/n.
For a finite event E, summing 1/n over E gives |E|/n.
repair_templates: Either justify equal likelihood on the chosen sample space or change to a sample space with correct outcome weights.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Countable discrete distribution
statement: For a countably infinite sample space, a discrete distribution assigns nonnegative masses whose infinite sum converges to 1, and event probabilities are obtained by convergent sums over event outcomes.
conditions: Omega is finite or countably infinite.
m(omega) >= 0 for every omega.
The series sum_{omega in Omega} m(omega) converges to 1.
E is a subset of Omega.
conclusion: P(E) is the sum of m(omega) over omega in E when the sum is defined by the distribution.
typical_uses: Check geometric, Poisson, and other countable probability models.
Repair proofs that use infinite sums without convergence or normalization.
common_misuses: Ignoring convergence of the infinite total mass.
Assigning positive equal mass to every positive integer.
Rearranging conditionally convergent sums as if all terms were nonnegative normalized masses.
bridge_lemmas: A nonnegative series has well-defined partial sums increasing to its total.
An event sum is bounded above by the total mass 1.
repair_templates: Add a proof that the nonnegative mass series sums to 1 before using it as a distribution.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Continuous density function
statement: A density function f for a real-valued continuous random variable gives interval probabilities by integrating f over the interval.
conditions: X is a continuous real-valued random variable considered with a density f.
a and b are real numbers with a <= b.
conclusion: P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b f(x) dx.
typical_uses: Compute continuous probabilities as areas under a density.
Repair proofs that treat density values as point probabilities.
common_misuses: Interpreting f(x) itself as P(X=x).
Using a function as a density without checking nonnegativity and total integral 1.
Forgetting domain restrictions where f is zero.
bridge_lemmas: For suitable events E, P(X in E)=integral_E f(x) dx.
Single points have probability 0 for ordinary continuous densities.
repair_templates: Replace point-probability claims with interval or event integrals and verify that f integrates to 1.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: CDF and density relation
statement: For a continuous random variable with density f, the cumulative distribution function is the integral of f from negative infinity to x, and where differentiable its derivative is f.
conditions: X is a continuous real-valued random variable with density f.
The relevant derivative exists at x.
conclusion: F(x)=integral_{-infinity}^x f(t) dt and F'(x)=f(x) at differentiability points.
typical_uses: Move between CDFs and densities.
Repair calculations of probabilities by using F(b)-F(a).
common_misuses: Differentiating a CDF at a discontinuity and calling it a density.
Assuming every CDF has an ordinary density.
Forgetting that P(a < X <= b)=F(b)-F(a).
bridge_lemmas: P(X <= x)=P(X in (-infinity,x]).
The fundamental theorem of calculus links the integral CDF to the density.
repair_templates: When a proof uses a density, define F by integration or verify F is differentiable with the claimed derivative.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Permutation and k-permutation counts
statement: A finite set with n elements has n! permutations, and the number of ordered selections of k distinct elements is n!/(n-k)! when 0 <= k <= n.
conditions: A is a finite set with n elements.
k is an integer with 0 <= k <= n.
conclusion: The number of permutations of A is n!, and the number of k-permutations is n(n-1)...(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!.
typical_uses: Compute sample-space sizes for ordered sampling without replacement.
Repair counting proofs that forget order or distinctness.
common_misuses: Using n^k when selections must be without replacement.
Using combinations when order matters.
Applying the formula with k > n.
bridge_lemmas: After each ordered choice without replacement, one fewer element remains.
The product rule multiplies the number of choices at successive stages.
repair_templates: State whether order matters and whether replacement is allowed, then choose n!/(n-k)! only for ordered distinct selections.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Stirling approximation
statement: For large n, n! is asymptotic to sqrt(2*pi*n) n^n e^{-n}.
conditions: n tends to infinity through positive integers.
conclusion: n! ~ sqrt(2*pi*n) n^n e^{-n}.
typical_uses: Approximate factorials in binomial and normal-limit calculations.
Repair asymptotic proofs of local central limit estimates.
common_misuses: Using Stirling for small n without error control.
Dropping the square-root factor when it matters for constants.
Applying asymptotic equivalence as exact equality.
bridge_lemmas: If a_n ~ b_n and c_n ~ d_n with nonzero terms, then ratios and products may be combined carefully.
For fixed p in (0,1), np and nq tend to infinity as n tends to infinity.
repair_templates: Replace exact equalities by asymptotic equivalences and check all factorial arguments tend to infinity.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Binomial coefficient formula
statement: The number of j-element subsets of an n-element set is n choose j, equal to n!/(j!(n-j)!).
conditions: n and j are integers.
conclusion: C(n,j)=n!/(j!(n-j)!) counts the j-element subsets of an n-element set.
typical_uses: Count unordered choices in finite probability models.
Repair binomial probability derivations by separating choice count from probability weight.
common_misuses: Using the formula for ordered selections.
Omitting the boundary cases j=0 or j=n.
Forgetting to divide by j! after counting ordered selections.
bridge_lemmas: Each j-subset has j! orderings.
There are n!/(n-j)! ordered selections of j distinct elements.
repair_templates: If order is irrelevant, divide the ordered count by j!.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bernoulli trials process
statement: A Bernoulli trials process consists of repeated independent trials, each with two outcomes called success and failure, with constant success probability p.
conditions: There are n repeated trials.
Each trial has outcomes success or failure.
Each trial has success probability p and failure probability q=1-p.
Trials are mutually independent.
conclusion: The sequence is a Bernoulli trials process with parameters n and p.
typical_uses: Justify binomial probabilities and indicator-variable sums.
Check whether independence and identical success probability have both been established.
common_misuses: Using binomial formulas when success probabilities vary across trials.
Assuming trials are independent because they have the same marginal probability.
Treating sampling without replacement as Bernoulli trials without approximation.
bridge_lemmas: The probability of any fixed success-failure sequence with j successes is p^j q^{n-j}.
There are C(n,j) sequences with j successes.
repair_templates: Add independence and constant-p hypotheses, or replace the binomial model by the appropriate nonidentical or dependent model.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Binomial distribution for successes
statement: In n Bernoulli trials with success probability p, the probability of exactly j successes is C(n,j)p^j(1-p)^{n-j}.
conditions: Sn is the number of successes in n Bernoulli trials.
0 <= j <= n is an integer.
conclusion: P(Sn=j)=C(n,j)p^j q^{n-j}.
typical_uses: Compute exact probabilities for counts of successes.
Repair a proof that counts arrangements but forgets the probability of each arrangement.
common_misuses: Using the formula outside the range 0 <= j <= n.
Omitting the binomial coefficient.
Using p^j q^{n-j} when many orders are possible.
bridge_lemmas: Each sequence with j successes has probability p^j q^{n-j}.
The number of such sequences is C(n,j).
repair_templates: Multiply the probability of one success pattern by the number of success patterns.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Binomial theorem and row sum
statement: For nonnegative integer n, (a+b)^n equals the sum over j of C(n,j)a^j b^{n-j}; in particular, the nth row of Pascal's triangle sums to 2^n.
conditions: n is a nonnegative integer.
a and b are numbers in a commutative algebraic setting.
conclusion: (a+b)^n=sum_{j=0}^n C(n,j)a^j b^{n-j}, and sum_{j=0}^n C(n,j)=2^n.
typical_uses: Normalize binomial distributions.
Repair algebraic simplifications involving binomial probabilities.
common_misuses: Using the finite expansion for noninteger exponents without additional convergence conditions.
Mismatching powers a^j and b^{n-j}.
Forgetting the endpoint terms j=0 and j=n.
bridge_lemmas: Set a=b=1 to get the row sum.
Set a=p and b=q with p+q=1 to prove binomial probabilities sum to 1.
repair_templates: Check the exponent range and include all j from 0 to n.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite inclusion-exclusion
statement: For finitely many events, the probability of their union is the alternating sum of probabilities of all nonempty intersections.
conditions: A1,...,An are events in the same probability space.
n is finite.
conclusion: P(union_i Ai)=sum P(Ai)-sum P(Ai intersect Aj)+sum P(Ai intersect Aj intersect Ak)-...+(-1)^{n+1}P(A1 intersect ... intersect An).
typical_uses: Repair probability calculations for unions of several overlapping events.
Check derangement and at-least-one-event arguments.
common_misuses: Adding only individual probabilities when overlaps exist.
Stopping after pairwise intersections when triple intersections are nonzero.
Using inclusion-exclusion for an infinite family without convergence justification.
bridge_lemmas: Each outcome in exactly r of the events contributes 1 to the alternating count.
Finite sums allow rearrangement of terms.
repair_templates: List the relevant intersections by size and include terms until the n-fold intersection.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Conditional probability
statement: When P(F)>0, the conditional probability of E given F is the probability of E intersect F divided by P(F).
conditions: E and F are events in the same probability space.
conclusion: P(E|F)=P(E intersect F)/P(F).
typical_uses: Translate conditional statements into intersection probabilities.
Repair Bayes and independence arguments by exposing denominators.
common_misuses: Conditioning on an event of probability 0 in the discrete formula.
Confusing P(E|F) with P(F|E).
Dropping the intersection with the conditioning event.
bridge_lemmas: P(E intersect F)=P(E|F)P(F) when P(F)>0.
The conditional probability is computed inside the restricted event F.
repair_templates: Verify P(F)>0 and rewrite the conditional probability using the definition.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Criterion for independent events
statement: Two events are independent exactly when the probability of their intersection equals the product of their probabilities, with zero-probability events treated as independent by convention in the text.
conditions: E and F are events in the same probability space.
conclusion: E and F are independent iff P(E intersect F)=P(E)P(F).
typical_uses: Check whether a proof may multiply event probabilities.
Repair conditional probability claims by proving the product criterion.
common_misuses: Assuming disjoint nonzero events are independent.
Assuming intuitive unrelatedness proves independence without calculation.
Using pairwise independence as mutual independence for a larger family.
bridge_lemmas: If P(F)>0, P(E|F)=P(E) is equivalent to P(E intersect F)=P(E)P(F).
If E and F are disjoint and both have positive probability, they are not independent.
repair_templates: Insert a calculation of P(E intersect F) and compare it to P(E)P(F) before multiplying probabilities.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mutual independence of events
statement: A finite family of events is mutually independent when every subfamily has intersection probability equal to the product of its member probabilities.
conditions: A1,...,An are events in the same probability space.
For every nonempty subfamily, the intersection probability is considered.
conclusion: The family is mutually independent iff P(intersection_{i in I} Ai)=product_{i in I}P(Ai) for every nonempty index set I.
typical_uses: Check whether products over more than two event probabilities are justified.
Repair proofs that verify only pairwise independence.
common_misuses: Treating pairwise independence as mutual independence.
Checking only the full intersection and ignoring smaller subfamilies.
Assuming complements are independent without first having mutual independence.
bridge_lemmas: For mutually independent events, replacing some events by complements preserves the corresponding product formula.
The full product condition alone does not imply mutual independence.
repair_templates: Add verification for every required subfamily or cite a theorem giving mutual independence from the model.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Joint discrete random variable
statement: Given random variables X1,...,Xn, their joint random variable takes ordered tuples of their values, with joint probabilities assigned on the Cartesian product of the individual value sets.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are random variables associated with one experiment.
Ri is the set of possible values of Xi.
conclusion: The joint random variable (X1,...,Xn) has sample space R1 x ... x Rn and a joint distribution on that space.
typical_uses: Repair proofs involving several random variables by introducing the joint distribution.
Check whether marginal probabilities are enough or joint probabilities are required.
common_misuses: Assuming all tuples in the Cartesian product have positive probability.
Multiplying marginals without independence.
Ignoring impossible tuples that must have probability 0.
bridge_lemmas: Marginal probabilities are obtained by summing joint probabilities over the other coordinates.
A joint distribution determines each marginal distribution.
repair_templates: Write the joint sample space and assign zero mass to impossible tuples before computing marginal or conditional probabilities.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Independent discrete random variables
statement: Discrete random variables X1,...,Xn are mutually independent when every joint point probability factors as the product of the corresponding marginal point probabilities.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are discrete random variables on the same probability space.
r1,...,rn are possible values of the variables.
conclusion: P(X1=r1,...,Xn=rn)=product_i P(Xi=ri) for all choices of ri.
typical_uses: Justify product distributions and computations for sums of independent variables.
Repair arguments that multiply probabilities for random-variable values.
common_misuses: Checking only one tuple of values.
Assuming uncorrelated or equal distributions imply independence.
Multiplying marginal probabilities when variables are functions of one another.
bridge_lemmas: If the factorization holds for all value tuples, the joint distribution is the product of the marginals.
Independence of variables implies independence of events determined separately by those variables.
repair_templates: Verify factorization for all relevant value combinations or cite the construction as an independent trials process.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Independent trials process
statement: A sequence of random variables is an independent trials process when the variables are mutually independent and have the same distribution.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are random variables.
The variables are mutually independent.
All Xi have the same distribution.
conclusion: X1,...,Xn form an independent trials process.
typical_uses: Justify using common means, variances, convolutions, LLN, or CLT for repeated experiments.
Repair arguments that need both independence and identical distribution.
common_misuses: Using independent-trials results for merely independent but nonidentically distributed variables.
Using the model for dependent sampling without replacement.
Assuming identical distribution proves independence.
bridge_lemmas: The product distribution on repeated trials gives mutual independence.
Coordinate random variables on a product sample space have the common trial distribution.
repair_templates: Add separate checks for mutual independence and identical marginal distribution.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bayes formula for finite hypotheses
statement: For a finite partition of hypotheses, the posterior probability of a hypothesis given evidence equals its prior times likelihood divided by the total likelihood-weighted prior mass.
conditions: H1,...,Hm are pairwise disjoint events whose union is Omega.
E is an event with P(E)>0.
P(Hi) and P(E|Hi) are known for each i with P(Hi)>0 when conditioning is used.
conclusion: P(Hi|E)=P(Hi)P(E|Hi)/sum_k P(Hk)P(E|Hk).
typical_uses: Repair inverse-probability arguments and diagnostic-test calculations.
Check that a proof has normalized posterior probabilities.
common_misuses: Confusing P(Hi|E) with P(E|Hi).
Omitting the denominator total probability of E.
Using nonexhaustive or overlapping hypotheses.
bridge_lemmas: P(E)=sum_k P(Hk intersect E).
P(Hk intersect E)=P(Hk)P(E|Hk).
repair_templates: State the hypothesis partition, compute the denominator by total probability, then divide each prior-likelihood product by it.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Joint density for continuous variables
statement: A joint density for continuous random variables assigns probabilities to regions by integrating the density over those regions in the variables' joint space.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are continuous random variables with joint density f.
E is a region for which the multiple integral is defined.
conclusion: P((X1,...,Xn) in E)=integral_E f(x1,...,xn) dx1...dxn.
typical_uses: Repair multivariable continuous probability calculations.
Check whether integration is over the correct region.
common_misuses: Multiplying marginal densities without independence.
Integrating over a rectangle when the event is not rectangular.
Treating joint density values as probabilities.
bridge_lemmas: Marginal densities are obtained by integrating the joint density over the other variables.
A valid joint density is nonnegative and integrates to 1 over the full space.
repair_templates: Write the event as a region in joint coordinates and integrate the joint density over that region.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Continuous independence by density factorization
statement: Continuous random variables are mutually independent when their joint density factors as the product of their marginal densities.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are continuous random variables with joint density f.
Each Xi has marginal density fi.
The factorization is asserted for all relevant points, except possibly a set irrelevant to integration.
conclusion: X1,...,Xn are independent iff f(x1,...,xn)=product_i fi(xi) in the density sense used for probabilities.
typical_uses: Justify product densities and separate multiple integrals.
Repair proofs that assume independence from unrelated-looking formulas.
common_misuses: Factoring only on part of the support.
Ignoring support restrictions that couple variables.
Assuming zero covariance implies density factorization.
bridge_lemmas: For independent variables, probabilities of rectangles factor as products of marginal probabilities.
Marginal densities come from integrating the joint density.
repair_templates: Compute marginal densities and verify the joint density equals their product on the full support.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Standard discrete distribution patterns
statement: Common discrete models include binomial counts of successes, geometric waiting time to first success, negative binomial waiting to kth success, hypergeometric sampling without replacement, and Poisson rare-event counts.
conditions: The random variable matches the stated model assumptions: independent Bernoulli trials for binomial or geometric models, sampling without replacement for hypergeometric models, or rare independent events with limiting rate lambda for Poisson models.
conclusion: Use the corresponding standard mass function and support for the random variable.
typical_uses: Identify a reusable distribution instead of deriving every mass function from scratch.
Repair model-selection errors in probability computations.
common_misuses: Using binomial instead of hypergeometric for sampling without replacement.
Using geometric formulas with inconsistent support convention.
Using Poisson approximation when event probabilities are not small or the rate is not controlled.
bridge_lemmas: A count model needs a support check before applying a named distribution.
The mass function must sum to 1 on its support.
repair_templates: Match the experiment assumptions to the named distribution, state the support, then write the mass function.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Standard continuous density patterns
statement: Common continuous models include uniform densities on intervals, exponential waiting-time densities, normal densities, and related transformed densities; probabilities are computed by integrating the relevant density over the event.
conditions: The random variable is continuous and its support and density match the chosen standard model.
The density is nonnegative and integrates to 1 on its support.
conclusion: The standard density may be used to compute probabilities, moments, and transformations for that model.
typical_uses: Repair continuous probability solutions by replacing informal area claims with a named density and integral.
Check model assumptions for waiting times or normal approximations.
common_misuses: Using a normal density outside an approximation context without justification.
Forgetting support restrictions for uniform or exponential densities.
Confusing density height with probability.
bridge_lemmas: For a density f, P(a<=X<=b)=integral_a^b f.
A transformed density may require a Jacobian or CDF method.
repair_templates: State the density and support explicitly, then compute the desired probability by integration.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Density transformation by monotone change of variable
statement: For a one-to-one differentiable transformation Y=phi(X), the density of Y is obtained by evaluating the density of X at the inverse image and multiplying by the absolute derivative of the inverse.
conditions: X has density fX.
Y=phi(X).
phi is one-to-one and differentiable on the relevant support, with differentiable inverse on the range.
The derivative of the inverse exists where the density is evaluated.
conclusion: fY(y)=fX(phi^{-1}(y))*|(phi^{-1})'(y)| on the range of Y, and 0 off the range.
typical_uses: Repair transformed-density calculations for scaling, shifting, powers, and simulations from CDFs.
Check missing Jacobian factors.
common_misuses: Forgetting the absolute value of the derivative.
Applying a one-to-one formula to a nonmonotone transformation without summing over branches.
Ignoring the transformed support.
bridge_lemmas: CDF method: P(Y<=y)=P(phi(X)<=y) with inequality direction depending on monotonicity.
Differentiating the transformed CDF yields the density.
repair_templates: Find the inverse, determine the new support, and include the absolute inverse-derivative factor; for multiple preimages, sum branch contributions.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Inverse CDF sampling
statement: If U is uniform on [0,1] and F is a continuous strictly increasing CDF with inverse F^{-1}, then F^{-1}(U) has CDF F.
conditions: U is uniformly distributed on [0,1].
F is a valid continuous strictly increasing cumulative distribution function on its range.
F^{-1} is defined on (0,1).
conclusion: The random variable X=F^{-1}(U) has cumulative distribution function F.
typical_uses: Generate random variables with a desired continuous distribution.
Repair simulation proofs by connecting a uniform source to the target CDF.
common_misuses: Using an inverse where F is not one-to-one without a generalized inverse.
Ignoring endpoints or support restrictions.

statement: In a finite absorbing Markov chain, the probability of eventual absorption is 1.
conditions: The Markov chain is finite and absorbing in the sense that every nonabsorbing state can reach an absorbing state.
Q is the transient-to-transient submatrix.
conclusion: Q^n tends to the zero matrix, and absorption occurs with probability 1 from any transient starting state.
typical_uses: Justify summing expected visits over all time.
Repair arguments that assume absorption without proving chain structure.
common_misuses: Applying the result to an infinite chain without extra conditions.
Using it when a closed nonabsorbing class exists.
Assuming absorption occurs within a fixed bounded time with probability 1.
bridge_lemmas: From each transient state there is a bounded positive probability of absorption within a fixed number of steps after taking a maximum over finitely many states.
Repeated failure probabilities are bounded by powers of a number less than 1.
repair_templates: Show the chain is finite and every transient state reaches absorption, then conclude Q^n -> 0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Fundamental matrix for absorbing chains
statement: For an absorbing Markov chain with transient submatrix Q, N=(I-Q)^{-1}=I+Q+Q^2+...; its ij entry is the expected number of visits to transient state j when starting in transient state i.
conditions: The finite Markov chain is absorbing.
Q is the transient-to-transient submatrix in canonical form.
N=(I-Q)^{-1} exists.
conclusion: N exists, equals the infinite matrix series, and N_{ij} is the expected number of visits to transient state sj from transient start si, counting the initial state when i=j.
typical_uses: Compute expected visits before absorption.
Repair absorbing-chain solutions that invert the wrong matrix.
common_misuses: Using P instead of Q in I-Q.
Forgetting that N counts visits to transient states only.
Not counting the initial state in diagonal entries when the theorem's convention does.
bridge_lemmas: Q^n -> 0 in an absorbing chain.
The finite geometric identity (I-Q)(I+...+Q^n)=I-Q^{n+1} leads to the inverse.
repair_templates: Put P in canonical form, extract Q, compute N=(I-Q)^{-1}, then interpret row i entries as expected visits.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Expected time to absorption
statement: In an absorbing Markov chain, the expected number of steps before absorption from each transient state is the corresponding row sum of the fundamental matrix.
conditions: The chain is finite and absorbing.
N is the fundamental matrix for transient states.
c is a column vector of ones.
conclusion: The vector t of expected absorption times is t=Nc.
typical_uses: Compute expected duration before absorption.
Repair proofs that confuse absorption probabilities with absorption times.
common_misuses: Including absorbing-state rows in N.
Forgetting to sum over all transient states.
Interpreting row sums as probabilities rather than expected counts.
bridge_lemmas: The expected time before absorption equals the expected total number of visits to transient states.
Row sums of N add expected visits over all transient states.
repair_templates: After computing N, multiply by the all-ones column vector to obtain expected times.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Absorption probabilities matrix
statement: In canonical form, the matrix of probabilities of eventual absorption in each absorbing state is B=NR.
conditions: The chain is finite and absorbing in canonical form.
Q is the transient-to-transient submatrix.
R is the transient-to-absorbing submatrix.
conclusion: B=NR, where B_{ij} is the probability of eventual absorption in absorbing state j starting from transient state i.
typical_uses: Compute absorption probabilities for gambler's ruin and finite absorbing chains.
Repair solutions that use expected visit counts but omit final transition probabilities.

Multiplying matrices in the wrong order.
Including absorbing rows in R.
bridge_lemmas: Expected visits to transient state k from i are N_{ik}.
Each visit to k has transition probability R_{kj} into absorbing state j on the next step.
repair_templates: Compute N from Q, extract R, then multiply N by R to get absorption probabilities.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Limit of a regular Markov chain
statement: For a finite regular Markov chain, powers of the transition matrix converge to a matrix with identical rows equal to a strictly positive probability vector.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite regular Markov chain.
conclusion: P^n tends to a matrix W whose rows are all the same strictly positive probability vector w.
typical_uses: Justify long-run state probabilities independent of the starting state.
Repair limiting-distribution arguments for regular chains.

Assuming convergence of P^n for every irreducible chain without aperiodicity.
Forgetting that w must be normalized.
bridge_lemmas: Regularity means some power of P has all positive entries.
Repeated averaging by P reduces dependence on the starting state.
repair_templates: Verify regularity or use the ergodic average theorem instead of the ordinary power limit.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Stationary vector for a regular chain
statement: For a regular transition matrix, the limiting row vector is the unique probability row vector satisfying wP=w; fixed row vectors are multiples of it.
conditions: P is a finite regular transition matrix.
w is a row probability vector.
conclusion: w is the limiting distribution iff wP=w; it is unique among probability row vectors.

Normalization turns a positive fixed row vector into a probability vector.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Regular chain forgets initial distribution
statement: For a regular Markov chain, any initial probability vector converges under repeated multiplication by P to the unique stationary distribution.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite regular Markov chain.
v is any initial probability row vector.
w is the unique fixed probability vector.
conclusion: vP^n tends to w as n tends to infinity.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Stationary distribution for ergodic chain
statement: A finite ergodic Markov chain has a unique strictly positive stationary probability vector, and all fixed row vectors are multiples of it.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite ergodic Markov chain.
conclusion: There is a unique strictly positive probability vector w with wP=w.

A fixed probability vector is normalized by sum_i w_i=1.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

statement: For a finite ergodic Markov chain, the average of I,P,...,P^n converges to a matrix with every row equal to the stationary distribution.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite ergodic Markov chain.
w is the unique stationary probability vector.
conclusion: An tends to W, where every row of W equals w.

name: Law of large numbers for ergodic Markov chains
statement: In a finite ergodic Markov chain, the empirical proportion of time spent in a state converges in probability to that state's stationary probability, independent of the starting state.
conditions: The Markov chain is finite and ergodic.
w is its unique stationary probability vector.
H_j^(n) is the proportion of the first n steps spent in state sj.
epsilon > 0.

statement: For a finite ergodic Markov chain, the mean return time to a state equals the reciprocal of its stationary probability.

w_j is the stationary probability of state sj.
r_j is the mean recurrence time to sj when starting at sj.
conclusion: r_j=1/w_j.

Cycles between returns to sj have average length r_j.

name: Simple random walk from iid increments
statement: A random walk is formed by summing independent identically distributed increments, often with symmetric step distributions in Euclidean space.

S0 is a starting point, often 0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Even-time return probability for one-dimensional symmetric walk
statement: For the simple symmetric random walk on the line, return to the origin can occur only at even times, and the 2m-step return probability is C(2m,m)/2^{2m}.
conditions: The random walk starts at 0 on the integer line.
Each step is +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 independently.
m is a nonnegative integer.

There are C(2m,m) such step sequences among 2^{2m} equally likely sequences.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: First-return decomposition for random walks
statement: Return probabilities can be decomposed by the time of first return, giving a convolution relation between first-return probabilities and ordinary return probabilities.
conditions: A random walk starts at the origin.
u_n is the probability of being at the origin at time n.
f_n is the probability of first return to the origin at time n.
conclusion: For n>=1, u_n=sum_{k=1}^n f_k u_{n-k}; in the symmetric nearest-neighbor line walk only even indices are nonzero.

Compute first-return probabilities from return probabilities.

Omitting the post-first-return segment in the convolution.

After first return, the future walk restarts probabilistically from the origin.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Gambler's ruin boundary-value method
statement: Finite gambler's ruin probabilities and expected durations are found by conditioning on the first step, yielding linear difference equations with boundary values at the absorbing fortunes.
conditions: A gambler's fortune moves by +1 with probability p and -1 with probability q=1-p until hitting 0 or N.
The chain starts at fortune i with 0 <= i <= N.
The desired quantity is an absorption probability or expected hitting time.
conclusion: The quantity satisfies a second-order linear recurrence in i with boundary conditions at 0 and N; solving the recurrence gives the desired probability or expectation.
typical_uses: Repair gambler's ruin proofs by deriving equations from first-step analysis.

Using the fair-game solution when p != q.
Writing the recurrence for interior states but applying it at the boundaries.

Absorption probabilities have boundary values 0 or 1 depending on the target boundary.

name: Convert between odds and probability
statement: If an event has probability p, its odds in favor are r:s with r/s=p/(1-p); conversely odds r:s correspond to probability r/(r+s).
conditions: E is an event.
0 <= P(E) < 1 for finite odds in favor.
r and s are nonnegative odds weights with r+s>0 for the inverse conversion.
conclusion: Odds and probabilities are related by r/s=p/(1-p) and p=r/(r+s).
typical_uses: Repair arguments that mix betting odds with event probabilities.
Check fair-bet calculations.

Ignoring the p=1 case where odds in favor are infinite.
Using odds against as if they were odds in favor.

P(E complement)=1-P(E).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Tree diagram path probability
statement: In a staged experiment, the probability of a complete path is the product of the conditional probabilities on its branches, and event probabilities are sums over the paths in the event.
conditions: The experiment is represented by a finite probability tree.
Each branch probability is conditional on the previous branches on that path.
The event is a set of terminal paths.
conclusion: The probability of a terminal path is the product of its branch probabilities, and the probability of an event is the sum of its terminal path probabilities.
typical_uses: Repair two-stage and multistage probability calculations.
Check Bayes tree computations and urn models.

Multiplying unconditional probabilities when later branch probabilities are conditional.

Distinct terminal paths are disjoint outcomes.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Discrete conditional distribution
statement: Conditioning a finite or countable discrete distribution on an event E with positive probability sets masses outside E to zero and renormalizes masses inside E by P(E).
conditions: Omega is a discrete sample space with mass function m.
E is an event with P(E)>0.
omega is an outcome in Omega.
conclusion: m(omega|E)=m(omega)/P(E) for omega in E and m(omega|E)=0 for omega not in E.

Check that probabilities after conditioning sum to 1.

Leaving positive probability on outcomes outside E.
Conditioning on an event of probability 0.

For any F, P(F|E)=sum_{omega in F intersect E}m(omega)/P(E).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Reverse tree for Bayes probabilities
statement: A two-stage probability tree can be reversed by preserving terminal path probabilities and dividing by first-level totals in the reversed order.
conditions: A two-stage experiment has terminal paths with known probabilities.
The target reversed first-stage event has positive total probability.

Dividing by the wrong marginal probability.

A conditional branch probability equals joint path probability divided by the conditioning event probability.

E is an event with P(E)>0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

p is the success probability and q=1-p.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Continuous uniform density on an interval

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

x >= 0 for the stated CDF and survival formulas.

r>=0 and s>=0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

statement: If Z is standard normal, then X=sigma Z+mu has normal density with center mu and standard deviation sigma, and normal probabilities reduce to standard normal probabilities by (x-mu)/sigma.
conditions: Z has standard normal density.
sigma>0.
X=sigma Z+mu.
conclusion: X has density (1/(sqrt(2*pi)*sigma)) exp(-(x-mu)^2/(2 sigma^2)), and P(X<=x)=P(Z<=(x-mu)/sigma).
typical_uses: Repair normal probability calculations and CLT standardizations.
Convert between general and standard normal tables.
common_misuses: Dividing by sigma^2 instead of sigma when standardizing.
Using a negative or zero standard deviation.
Forgetting to transform both interval endpoints.
bridge_lemmas: A linear increasing change of variable contributes inverse derivative 1/sigma.
The standard normal CDF tabulates P(Z<=z).
repair_templates: Set z=(x-mu)/sigma for each endpoint and compute the corresponding standard normal probability.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Expected number of records by indicators
statement: For iid continuous observations with no ties, the probability that the jth observation is a new record among the first j observations is 1/j, so the expected number of records in n observations is the nth harmonic sum.
conditions: The first n observations are exchangeable, for example iid from a continuous distribution.
Ties have probability 0.
Xj is the indicator that observation j is the maximum among observations 1,...,j.
conclusion: E(Xj)=1/j and E(sum_{j=1}^n Xj)=sum_{j=1}^n 1/j.
typical_uses: Repair expected-count proofs by indicator decomposition and symmetry.
Check record-value arguments.
common_misuses: Assuming independence of record indicators is needed for expectation.
Using 1/n for every j instead of 1/j.
Ignoring ties in discrete data.
bridge_lemmas: By symmetry, each of the first j observations is equally likely to be the maximum.
Linearity of expectation adds the indicator expectations.
repair_templates: Define record indicators, prove E(Xj)=P(Xj=1)=1/j by symmetry, and sum over j.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Variance of Bernoulli count and proportion
statement: For n Bernoulli trials with success probability p, the success count has variance np(1-p), and the sample proportion has variance p(1-p)/n.
conditions: Sn is the sum of n independent Bernoulli(p) indicators.
An=Sn/n.
conclusion: V(Sn)=npq and V(An)=pq/n.
typical_uses: Repair LLN and polling standard-error calculations.
Check variance used in binomial normal approximations.
common_misuses: Using np for the variance instead of npq.
Using pq/n for the count rather than the proportion.
Forgetting independence of the Bernoulli indicators.
bridge_lemmas: A Bernoulli(p) indicator X satisfies E(X)=p and E(X^2)=p.
The variance of independent sums adds and scaling by 1/n divides variance by n^2.
repair_templates: Compute the single-indicator variance pq, add over n trials for Sn, then scale for An.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mean and variance of geometric waiting time
statement: For the first-success trial number T in Bernoulli(p) trials, E(T)=1/p and V(T)=(1-p)/p^2.
conditions: T has the geometric distribution on {1,2,...} with P(T=j)=q^{j-1}p.
0<p<1 and q=1-p.
conclusion: E(T)=1/p and V(T)=q/p^2.
typical_uses: Repair waiting-time expectation and variance calculations.
Check queueing or repeated-trial models.
common_misuses: Using q/p as the variance.
Using the formulas for a different support convention without adjustment.
Applying the mean 1/p to nonidentical trials.
bridge_lemmas: Differentiate the geometric series to compute sums of j q^{j-1} and j^2 q^{j-1}.
repair_templates: Confirm T counts the success trial itself; if it counts failures before success, shift by 1 and adjust moments.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mean and variance of Poisson distribution
statement: A Poisson random variable with parameter lambda has both mean and variance equal to lambda.
conditions: X has Poisson distribution with mass e^{-lambda}lambda^j/j! on j>=0.
lambda>0.
conclusion: E(X)=lambda and V(X)=lambda.
typical_uses: Repair moment calculations for Poisson counts.
Check Poisson approximations and dispersion assumptions.
common_misuses: Treating lambda as a standard deviation.
Assuming variance equals lambda^2.
Using the formula for non-Poisson count data without model justification.
bridge_lemmas: The Poisson moment generating function is exp(lambda(e^t-1)).
Differentiate the MGF at 0 to get the first two moments.
repair_templates: Identify lambda as the expected count, then set both mean and variance equal to lambda.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Sample variance bias correction
statement: For iid observations with variance sigma^2, the sample variance using coefficient 1/n has expectation ((n-1)/n)sigma^2, while using 1/(n-1) gives an unbiased estimator of sigma^2.
conditions: X1,...,Xn are iid with mean mu and variance sigma^2.
The sample mean is xbar=(1/n)sum_i Xi.
The uncorrected sample variance is (1/n)sum_i (Xi-xbar)^2.
conclusion: E[(1/n)sum_i (Xi-xbar)^2]=((n-1)/n)sigma^2, and E[(1/(n-1))sum_i (Xi-xbar)^2]=sigma^2.
typical_uses: Repair statistical proof steps involving unbiased variance estimation.
Check whether a sample-variance formula uses the intended denominator.
common_misuses: Calling the 1/n sample variance unbiased for sigma^2.
Using the n-1 correction when n=1.
Forgetting that xbar is random and consumes one degree of freedom.
bridge_lemmas: sum_i (Xi-xbar)^2 = sum_i (Xi-mu)^2 - n(xbar-mu)^2.
E((xbar-mu)^2)=sigma^2/n.
repair_templates: Replace denominator n by n-1 when an unbiased estimator of sigma^2 is required.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic
statement: For observed counts oi and expected counts ei under a finite categorical model, the statistic sum_i (oi-ei)^2/ei is compared to a chi-square distribution with appropriate degrees of freedom when expected counts are adequate.
conditions: Data are counts in finitely many categories.
The null model specifies expected counts ei>0.
Observed counts oi have the same total count as the expected counts.
The chi-square approximation conditions are appropriate for the model.
conclusion: Large values of V=sum_i (oi-ei)^2/ei provide evidence against the hypothesized categorical distribution.
typical_uses: Repair arguments testing fairness of dice or categorical models.
Check that expected counts, not probabilities alone, are used in the statistic.
common_misuses: Using probabilities pi in the denominator instead of expected counts n pi.
Applying the approximation with very small expected counts without caution.
Using the wrong degrees of freedom after estimating parameters.
bridge_lemmas: Under a uniform six-sided die model with n rolls, each expected count is n/6.
The statistic measures squared deviations scaled by expected frequencies.
repair_templates: Compute expected counts under the null, form sum (observed-expected)^2/expected, then compare to the correct chi-square reference distribution.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Moments from moment generating function
statement: When the moment generating function g(t)=E(e^{tX}) is defined near zero and termwise differentiation is justified, the kth moment is g^{(k)}(0).
conditions: g(t)=E(e^{tX}) exists in a neighborhood of t=0 or the finite-range/formal calculation justifies differentiation.
k is a nonnegative integer.
conclusion: E(X^k)=g^{(k)}(0). In particular, E(X)=g'(0) and V(X)=g''(0)-[g'(0)]^2.
typical_uses: Repair mean and variance computations using MGFs.
Check that MGF manipulations are justified.
common_misuses: Differentiating an MGF that does not exist near zero.
Confusing raw moments with central moments.
Using g''(0) directly as variance without subtracting the square of the mean.
bridge_lemmas: The exponential series has coefficients X^k/k!.
For valid MGFs, differentiation extracts power-series coefficients.
repair_templates: Verify MGF existence or finite support, differentiate the MGF, evaluate at zero, and compute variance from the first two raw moments.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: MGF under shifts and scaling
statement: If Y=X+a then g_Y(t)=e^{at}g_X(t), and if Y=bX then g_Y(t)=g_X(bt), wherever the MGFs are defined.
conditions: X has an MGF g_X on the needed values of t.
a and b are constants.
Y is X+a or bX.
conclusion: The MGF transforms by multiplication by e^{at} for shifts and by argument scaling for multiplication by b.
typical_uses: Repair standardization and affine-transform MGF calculations.
Derive distributions or moments after linear transformations.
common_misuses: Using e^a instead of e^{at} for a shift.
Multiplying the MGF by b for scaling instead of replacing t by bt.
Ignoring the domain where the MGF exists.
bridge_lemmas: e^{t(X+a)}=e^{at}e^{tX}.
e^{t(bX)}=e^{(bt)X}.
repair_templates: Rewrite e^{tY} algebraically in terms of X, then take expectation.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Generating function of independent sum
statement: The moment generating function, and for nonnegative integer variables the ordinary generating function, of a sum of independent random variables is the product of the individual generating functions.
conditions: X and Y are independent random variables.
Z=X+Y.
The relevant generating functions exist or are valid as formal power series.
conclusion: g_Z(t)=g_X(t)g_Y(t), and for nonnegative integer-valued variables h_Z(z)=h_X(z)h_Y(z).
typical_uses: Repair convolution calculations by using generating functions.
Prove that sums of independent binomial, Poisson, or related variables have expected distributions.
common_misuses: Multiplying generating functions without independence.
Using ordinary generating functions for noninteger-valued variables without modification.
Forgetting that coefficient extraction is still needed to recover probabilities.
bridge_lemmas: Independence gives E(e^{tX}e^{tY})=E(e^{tX})E(e^{tY}).
For integer-valued variables, z^{X+Y}=z^X z^Y.
repair_templates: Establish independence, multiply the generating functions, then identify the resulting distribution or extract coefficients.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mean size of nth branching generation
statement: In a branching process with mean offspring number m per individual, the expected number of individuals in generation n is m^n when starting with one individual.
conditions: A Galton-Watson branching process starts with one individual.
Individuals reproduce independently with common offspring generating function h.
m=h'(1) is the mean number of offspring.
conclusion: E(Z_n)=m^n for generation n, using Z_0=1.
typical_uses: Repair branching-process expectation calculations.
Check supercritical, critical, and subcritical growth claims.
common_misuses: Interpreting E(Z_n)=m^n as almost sure growth.
Using the formula when reproduction laws vary by generation without modification.
Confusing extinction probability with expected population size.
bridge_lemmas: The generating function of generation n+1 is h_n(h(z)).
Differentiating at z=1 gives m_{n+1}=m_n m.
repair_templates: Compute m=h'(1), then use E(Z_n)=m^n only as an expectation statement.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: First-step equations for mean first passage
statement: Mean first passage and recurrence times in an ergodic Markov chain satisfy linear equations obtained by conditioning on the first transition.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite ergodic Markov chain.
m_ij is the expected steps to hit state j starting from i, with m_jj=0.
r_i is the expected return time to i.
conclusion: For i!=j, m_ij=1+sum_{k!=j} p_ik m_kj; and r_i=1+sum_k p_ik m_ki.
typical_uses: Repair hitting-time computations in Markov chains.
Set up linear systems for expected passage times.
common_misuses: Including the target state j term with m_jj incorrectly instead of using the boundary value 0.
Forgetting the +1 for the first step.
Using the equations in nonergodic chains without checking finiteness.
bridge_lemmas: Conditioning on the first step partitions by the next state.
If the first step hits the target, no additional passage time remains beyond that first step.
repair_templates: Define the target state, set m_jj=0, condition on the first step, include the initial +1, and solve the resulting linear system.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mean first passage from ergodic fundamental matrix
statement: For a finite ergodic Markov chain, Z=(I-P+W)^{-1} exists and mean first passage times are m_ij=(z_jj-z_ij)/w_j.
conditions: P is the transition matrix of a finite ergodic Markov chain.
w is the stationary row probability vector.
W is the matrix with every row equal to w.
i and j are states.
conclusion: The mean first passage time from i to j is m_ij=(z_jj-z_ij)/w_j, with m_jj=0 under the book's convention.
typical_uses: Compute hitting times in ergodic Markov chains without solving a separate system for each target.
Repair misuse of absorbing-chain fundamental matrices in ergodic settings.
common_misuses: Using (I-P)^{-1}, which does not exist for a stochastic matrix with stationary vector.
Forgetting to build W from the stationary distribution.
Using the formula before establishing ergodicity.
bridge_lemmas: I-P+W is invertible for finite ergodic chains.
Z(I-P)=I-W and Zc=c.
repair_templates: Find w, form W, compute Z=(I-P+W)^{-1}, then apply (z_jj-z_ij)/w_j for each passage time.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite gambler's ruin probability
statement: For a gambler starting with z dollars and absorbing barriers 0 and M, the probability of ruin before reaching M has an explicit formula from the first-step recurrence.
conditions: The fortune changes by +1 with probability p and -1 with probability q=1-p each play.
The process starts at integer z with 0<=z<=M.
The game stops when fortune hits 0 or M.
conclusion: If p!=q, P(ruin before M)=((q/p)^M-(q/p)^z)/((q/p)^M-1); if p=q=1/2, P(ruin before M)=(M-z)/M.
typical_uses: Check closed-form solutions of finite absorbing random walks.
Repair boundary-condition errors in gambler's ruin proofs.
common_misuses: Using the fair formula when p!=q.
Dropping the boundary cases z=0 or z=M.
Confusing ruin probability with success probability, which is one minus this value.
bridge_lemmas: The ruin probabilities satisfy q_z=p q_{z+1}+q q_{z-1} with q_0=1 and q_M=0.
Solving the recurrence uses a geometric sequence when p!=q and a linear sequence when p=q.
repair_templates: Write the recurrence with boundary values, solve the geometric or linear case, and verify the formula at z=0 and z=M.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ruin probability against infinitely rich adversary
statement: Against an infinitely rich adversary, a gambler with initial fortune z is eventually ruined with probability 1 if p<=q and with probability (q/p)^z if p>q.
conditions: The fortune changes by +1 with probability p and -1 with probability q=1-p each play.
The initial fortune z is a positive integer.
The adversary has no upper absorbing boundary.
conclusion: P(eventual ruin)=1 when p<=q, and P(eventual ruin)=(q/p)^z when p>q.
typical_uses: Repair infinite-barrier random-walk ruin arguments.
Check claims about favorable games and survival probability.
common_misuses: Assuming a favorable game p>q eliminates ruin probability entirely.
Using finite-M formulas without taking the limit M to infinity.
Forgetting that fair random walk still has ruin probability 1.
bridge_lemmas: Let the upper boundary M tend to infinity in the finite gambler's ruin formula.
If q/p<1, (q/p)^M tends to 0; if q/p>=1, the limiting ruin probability is 1.
repair_templates: Start from the finite-barrier formula and take M -> infinity, separating p>q from p<=q.
